newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl, Chirac to coordinate policy before Dublin summit.
newsitem.headline: Kohl, Chirac to coordinate policy before Dublin summit.

text.p: France and Germany, the troubled tandem leading the European Union towards greater integration, hold their six-monthly summit in Nuremberg on Monday to unveil their latest proposals for EU reform.

President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl, in what is now a tradition before important EU summits, plan to issue a letter to Friday's European Council in Dublin outlining their ideas for the bloc's intergovernmental conference (IGC).

"The letter will be a chance for the president and the chancellor to reaffirm once again the determination of Germany and France to face together the challenge of building Europe," French foreign ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt said.
Several key challenges, though, should be absent from the letter because Germany, France and their EU partners still cannot agree on them, officials in the two capitals say.

The toughest nut to crack is the stability pact Bonn has proposed to ensure that countries joining the planned economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999 stay on the path of budget discipline once the single euro currency is launched.

Germany wants a stringent pact, with automatic penalties for members whose overspending threatens the euro's stability, while France speaks for a majority of EU members arguing for a bit more leeway to decide who and when to punish.

Germany's hard negotiating line has prompted criticism abroad, especially in France where charges of a German "diktat" have been heard and former President Valery Giscard d'Estaing has called for a devaluation of the franc.

Officials say Kohl and Chirac, who met twice in France last week, agree on the essentials of the pact but their finance and economics ministers still have to work out details with their colleagues at a special EU meeting before the Dublin summit.
One way to diffuse tension over the stability pact would be to agree on a closer coordination of economic policies to ensure more is done to promote growth and jobs, they say.
Karl Lamers, foreign policy spokesman for Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), noted French proposals for Europe-wide economic policies to complement the monetary stability goal.
"(German Finance Minister) Theo Waigel has suggested a stability council - that's the same thing only under a different name," he said.

The Kohl-Chirac letter will focus rather on two other parts of the IGC reform due to be completed in mid-1997 -- reforms to further integrate foreign and defence policy as well as interior and justice affairs, a senior French official said.
France and Germany want to strengthen the EU's foreign policy standing by naming an official to coordinate national approaches into a single initiative.
They also hope to harmonise asylum and immigration policies and cooperate more closely in fighting organised crime, drug smuggling and terrorism.

A key element in furthering such cooperation, a so-called "flexibility clause" allowing some states to integrate faster than others in specific areas, has proven so contentious that the Irish presidency's draft IGC treaty avoids defining it.

Kohl and Chirac called for this flexibility at their summit in Baden-Baden a year ago, but Britain, wary of anything which smacks of surrendering more sovereignty to Brussels, is deeply suspicious of the plan.

Defence ministers Charles Millon and Volker Ruehe are due to review bilateral relations strained after Chirac scrapped conscription and reformed the French armed forces, a move making it harder for Bonn to retain its own draft.
Rhe also says he cannot afford to pay Bonn's share of the Helios 2 spy satellite France wants to build to make Europe less dependent on United States intelligence.
Diplomats said both sides were reviewing several joint arms projects with a view to having the defence industry help cut costs for their development and production.
